title: Data Loss Prevention
summary: Data loss prevention (DLP) is the set of controls that watch data in motion, in use and at rest, and block or record it when it crosses a boundary the organisation has defined. Detection combines content inspection, such as matching patterns for card numbers or national identifiers, with context such as the sender, the destination and the volume, because content alone produces far too much noise. DLP works best on a small number of high value categories with a named owner, and it usually starts in monitor mode so teams can tune rules before anything is blocked. The recurring mistake is buying a tool and treating its alerts as the programme; without classification, an incident process and user education, it generates queues nobody can work. It reduces accidental and careless loss and raises the cost of deliberate exfiltration, but it does not stop a determined insider who already has legitimate access.

beginner.definition: Data loss prevention means tools and rules that stop sensitive information from leaving your company by mistake. The tools watch files, emails and uploads, then warn, block or record what they see. They can only help if the company already knows which data is sensitive.
beginner.whyItMatters: People share information all day, and a small mistake can send a customer list to the wrong address. Once that data is outside, you cannot take it back. Rules that warn before sending give people a chance to stop. Records of what left the network also help you investigate later. Without these controls, a leak may go unseen for months.
howItWorks: The company decides which kinds of data need protection, such as card numbers or health records.
Rules describe how that data looks, and where it may or may not go.
The tool inspects email, file shares, web uploads and sometimes the device itself.
When a rule matches, the tool can warn the user, block the action or only record it.
A person reviews the alerts, and the rules are tuned to reduce false alarms.
Repeated mistakes lead to training, and deliberate attempts lead to an investigation.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office where staff must spot parcels that should not be sent abroad. A new rule says that any parcel with a medical label needs a manager's stamp. The clerk sees thousands of parcels a day, so a separate rule for every possible item would stop all work. The clerk learns a few clear signs instead, and asks when unsure. Sometimes the clerk stops a harmless parcel, and that small delay is accepted. When a parcel without the stamp slips through, the office reviews the day and improves the signs. Data loss prevention works like that, with a few good rules and steady tuning rather than perfect detection.
takeaways: Start by protecting a few high value data types, not everything at once.
Run new rules in recording mode before you block anything.
Give every alert a named owner, or the queue will be ignored.

objectives: Explain what data loss prevention is and which three states of data it covers.
Describe how content inspection and context work together to detect a leak.
Outline a staged rollout that starts in monitor mode and tunes rules before blocking.
Identify the operational tasks that keep a data loss prevention programme useful.
Recognise the limits of these tools against a determined insider.
